title: The pillars, reviewed
hook: five pillars, now understood from the inside

segments.voice: Yesterday, your balance, and your line: give each its right. Worship, work, rest and family, each with its share. Did you rest well last night, and give the rest its right too? Day one thousand four hundred twelve.

Five words fit on an index card: testimony, prayer, zakat, fasting, pilgrimage. A visitor to a mosque could learn the list over one cup of tea. This year did not stop at the card. It stayed a long while inside each pillar: the words of the testimony, the standing and bowing of the prayer, the arithmetic and the mercy of zakat, the long afternoons of the fast, the white cloth of the pilgrimage. Now the year is closing, and these last days gather what it taught, one part at a time. First, the pillars again, this time from the inside.
screen: `FIVE WORDS ON AN INDEX CARD.` → `A LONG WHILE INSIDE EACH ONE.` → `NOW, FROM THE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Start with the frame. In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says Islam is built on five: bearing witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger, establishing the prayer, giving zakat, the pilgrimage, and fasting Ramadan. Built on. A house, not a checklist. Now look at each one from the inside, using the texts themselves. The testimony is said with the tongue, and Muslim teachers say it has to be meant: words that count when they are sincere. The prayer: the Qur'an praises the believers "Who are humble in their prayers." The standing and bowing are the outside. That humility, khushu', is the inside. Zakat: the Qur'an tells the Prophet to take alms from people's wealth to purify them, in paraphrase. So the giving cleans the giver, not only feeds the poor. The fast: in Pickthall's Qur'an, fasting is prescribed "that ye may ward off (evil)." The hunger is the outside. The guarding is the inside. The pilgrimage: the Qur'an says the flesh and blood of the sacrifice do not reach Allah, but the devotion of the people does, in paraphrase. See the pattern. Each pillar has a body and a heart. In Muslim teaching, the body is required: the movements, the amounts, the days. And the texts keep pointing past the body to what it carries. That is what from the inside means. Not skipping the outside, but finding what it holds. One more thing the year showed: the pillars lean on each other. The prayer holds the day. The fast holds a month. The pilgrimage, for whoever is able, can hold a whole life.
screen: `BUILT ON FIVE: A HOUSE, NOT A LIST.` · `EACH PILLAR HAS A BODY AND A HEART.` · `HUMBLE IN PRAYER, GUARDED IN THE FAST.` · `THE PILLARS LEAN ON EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray on time today, or keep the time. Settle into the sit, and breathe. Bring to mind the next prayer of the day, the one coming after this lesson. If you pray, you can decide now where you will be when it comes, and plan to stop for it when it arrives, not after. If you don't pray, choose that same moment anyway, and when it comes, pause for one breath and remember that somewhere, someone is standing for that prayer just then. For now, rest here. The bell holds the time.
The pillars. The five things Islam is built on, in the hadith's words: testimony, prayer, zakat, pilgrimage and fasting, each with a body and a heart. Today's word.

Your line: from the inside. Today, pick one pillar and do one small piece of it with its inside in mind: one slow bow, or one gift given quietly. Tomorrow, the reports, reviewed. Day one thousand four hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Muslims keep the pillars as acts with set forms: saying the testimony, praying the daily prayers at their times, paying zakat on qualifying wealth, fasting the month of Ramadan, and making the Hajj if able; teachers stress the intention and humility behind each act.

fork.setup: the time for prayer comes while you're in the middle of work. today's line is "from the inside." which fits it?
options: skip the prayer and just think kind thoughts.
pray, and let the movements carry humility.

fork.reveal: the Qur'an praises those "who are humble in their prayers": the body and the heart together, not one instead of the other.

original.note: Arabic: pillars; the five are called arkan al-islam, the pillars of Islam.

trapdoor: what you thought: five rules on an index card.
what it means: five acts Islam is built on, each with an outward body and an inward heart.
what a scholar hears: buniya al-islam 'ala khams, built on five (Bukhari), and verses tying each act to an inner aim: humility, purity, guarding, devotion.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 8 (Islam is built on five)

notes: Confirm Pickthall's exact wording for 23:2 ('Who are humble in their prayers') and 2:183 ('that ye may ward off (evil)').
Bukhari 8 order is testimony, prayer, zakat, Hajj, fasting Ramadan; the hook uses the more familiar order for the list of five words. Confirm this is acceptable.
'Muslim teachers say [the testimony] has to be meant' and 'Muslims hold that the body is required' are general statements without a cited text; a Keeper should confirm the wording.
'The fast holds a month' rests on 2:185 (the month of Ramadan); not cited separately.
Original: arkan al-islam as the common name for the five; confirm.
Editor pass (2026-10-02): softened the general claim 'Muslims hold that the body is required' to 'In Muslim teaching'.
